title: Markdown Basics for Technical Documentation
text: Markdown is a simple way to format text without using complicated design software. It is commonly used for README files, documentation, and Quarto websites.

title: Markdown Basics for Technical Documentation
text:
Create Headings
Headings help organize information.
Use one # for a large heading and two ## symbols for a smaller heading.
# Main Heading

## Smaller Heading
Good headings make documentation easier to scan.

title: Markdown Basics for Technical Documentation
text:
Make Text Bold or Italic
Use two asterisks to make important text bold.
**Important information**
Use one asterisk for italic text.
*Helpful note*

title: Markdown Basics for Technical Documentation
text:
Create Lists
Use hyphens for bullet lists:
- First item
- Second item
- Third item
Use numbers when readers need to follow steps in order:
1. Open VS Code.
2. Create a file.
3. Save the file.

title: Markdown Basics for Technical Documentation
text:
Add Links
Links help readers find more information.
A Markdown link looks like this:
[Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/)

title: Markdown Basics for Technical Documentation
text:
Add Images
Images use similar syntax:
![Description of the image](images/example.png)
The words inside the square brackets are called alt text. Alt text describes the image for people who cannot see it.



VS Code showing a Markdown file and its preview

title: Markdown Basics for Technical Documentation
text:
Preview Markdown
VS Code can show a preview of a Markdown document. Open a Markdown file and use the preview command to compare the source text with the formatted result.
Markdown keeps the source file simple while still allowing you to create organized and readable documentation.

title: Getting Started with GitHub and VS Code
text: This guide explains how to create, publish, and collaborate on a simple documentation project using VS Code, GitHub Desktop, and GitHub Pages.

title: Getting Started with GitHub and VS Code
text:
1. Set Up VS Code
If your laptop is provided by the English Department at Iowa State University, install VS Code through the Self Help application. If you use a personal device, download Visual Studio Code.
After installing VS Code, open Extensions and install Markdown All in One. Extensions add useful features to VS Code.
See the VS Code extensions documentation.

title: Getting Started with GitHub and VS Code
section: 2. Set Up GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
2. Set Up GitHub and GitHub Desktop
Create a free GitHub account and install GitHub Desktop. If you use a department-owned laptop, contact IT if installation help is needed.
Sign in to GitHub Desktop with the same account. GitHub stores repositories online, while GitHub Desktop provides a visual way to manage changes.
See GitHub’s Hello World tutorial.

title: Getting Started with GitHub and VS Code
text:
3. Create and Publish a Repository
In GitHub Desktop:

Select File → New Repository.
Name and create the repository.
Click Publish repository.
Make sure it is public.

Open the repository in VS Code and create index.html at the top level. Add a link to the public repository:
<a href="https://github.com/snehab-hub/solo-doc-documentation">
  Link to repository
</a>
Save the file.

title: Getting Started with GitHub and VS Code
text:
4. Stage, Commit, and Push Changes
Open GitHub Desktop. Under Changes, select index.html. Enter a short commit message such as Add index page, then click Commit to main and Push origin.
A commit records a version of your work. Pushing sends that version to GitHub.

Remember: commit records the change; push sends it to GitHub.

See the GitHub Desktop commit guide.



GitHub Desktop showing project changes

title: Getting Started with GitHub and VS Code
text:
5. Publish with GitHub Pages
On GitHub, open Settings → Pages. Choose Deploy from a branch, select main and /(root), and click Save.
GitHub Pages turns index.html into a public website. Open the website URL and confirm that Link to repository appears and returns to your repository.
See the GitHub Pages documentation.

title: Getting Started with GitHub and VS Code
text:
6. Collaborate with a Pull Request
A pull request lets someone propose changes to a project without changing the main version right away.
Open Settings → Collaborators and invite another GitHub user. After they accept, ask them to create a branch, make a small change, commit it, and open a pull request.
Review the pull request, approve it, and merge it into main. Then use Fetch origin or Pull origin in GitHub Desktop to update your local copy.
See GitHub’s pull request documentation.

title: Building and Previewing a Quarto Website
text: Quarto is a publishing tool that can turn Markdown-based files into websites. Instead of writing every HTML page by hand, you write your content in .qmd files and let Quarto create the web pages.

title: Building and Previewing a Quarto Website
text:
Check That Quarto Is Installed
Open the terminal in Visual Studio Code.
Type:
quarto --version
If Quarto is installed correctly, the terminal will display a version number.

title: Building and Previewing a Quarto Website
text:
Create Quarto Pages
Quarto pages usually use the .qmd file extension.
For example:
index.qmd
markdown-basics.qmd
quarto-website.qmd
The index.qmd file normally becomes the home page of the website.

title: Building and Previewing a Quarto Website
text:
Preview the Website
Open the terminal in the main project folder.
Run:
quarto preview
Quarto will build the website and open a preview in your browser.



A Quarto website preview open in a browser


Keep the preview open while editing. When you save a file, Quarto can update the preview.

title: Building and Previewing a Quarto Website
text:
Stop the Preview
Go back to the VS Code terminal.
Press:
Ctrl + C
This stops the preview server.

title: Building and Previewing a Quarto Website
text:
Render the Website
When the site is ready, run:
quarto render
Quarto creates the finished HTML files for the website.
The generated website normally appears inside a folder called _site.

title: Building and Previewing a Quarto Website
text:
Publish the Site
After checking the rendered website, the project can be uploaded to GitHub and published with GitHub Pages.
Quarto allows the source content to remain separate from the final HTML website, which makes the project easier to edit and maintain.
